messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Factory Worker
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Vignette:
Marina is a 38-year-old Latina woman who works on the assembly line at a plastics factory on the outskirts of a midwestern city. She came to therapy at the urging of her younger sister, who had grown worried by the way Marina had been withdrawing from the family over the past year. Marina sat stiffly on the edge of the chair during the intake, her hands folded tightly in her lap, and she spoke in a low, careful voice as though she was afraid of what might come out if she let herself speak freely.

The traumatic event that changed everything for Marina happened fourteen months ago. Her older brother, Eduardo, had been riding his motorcycle home from his night shift at a warehouse when a driver ran a red light and struck him at an intersection. Marina received the call from her mother at 3:00 a.m. She remembers the sound of the phone ringing, the way her mother’s voice cracked as she said Eduardo’s name, and then the long, hollow silence that followed. By the time Marina reached the hospital, Eduardo was already gone. She never got to say goodbye. She never got to tell him that she loved him one more time. What stayed with her most vividly was the sound of the sirens she heard as she drove to the hospital—sirens that she now knows were probably for someone else, but that she has come to associate, irrevocably, with the moment her world broke apart.

In the months that followed, Marina found herself caught in a loop she could not escape. She would lie awake at night replaying the details of that phone call, the drive to the hospital, the look on her mother’s face. She went over and over the sequence of events, trying to find some logic in it, some reason that would make it feel less senseless. She would ask her sister, again and again, “Do you think he knew what was happening? Do you think he suffered?” Her sister would reassure her, would tell her that the doctors said it was instant, but Marina could never quite believe it. The reassurance lasted only a few hours before the doubt crept back in, and she would find herself asking the same questions all over again.

The world around Marina began to shrink. She stopped attending family gatherings because she knew someone would bring up Eduardo, and the thought of hearing his name spoken in the past tense made her chest tighten until she could barely breathe. When a coworker mentioned that her own aunt had passed away, Marina excused herself to the bathroom and stood gripping the sink, staring at her reflection, telling herself to get it together. She stopped driving past the cemetery where Eduardo was buried, even though it added twenty minutes to her commute. At the factory, the sound of a distant siren from a passing ambulance would freeze her mid-motion, her hands hovering over the machine, her heart pounding so hard she could hear it in her ears. She would have to step away from her station and pretend she was checking something in the back.

Marina had come to believe that she no longer belonged anywhere. Before Eduardo’s death, she had been the one who organized the family barbecues, who joked with her coworkers during lunch breaks, who looked forward to weekends. Now she felt like a ghost moving through her own life. She used to be a happy person, she told herself, but that person was gone. What frightened her most was the growing certainty that her life had been destroyed by the trauma, that there was no version of the future in which she would ever feel okay again. She had begun to wonder whether she was even capable of happiness anymore, or whether that part of her had died alongside her brother.

What finally brought Marina to seek help was a moment at work when a supervisor found her crying on the floor of the break room after a coworker had casually mentioned a news story about a family who had lost someone in a car accident. Marina could not explain why that particular comment had undone her. She had simply felt the floor give way beneath her, and she had sat down and let the tears come. Her supervisor, a kind woman who had lost her own husband years ago, told Marina quietly that she had been through something terrible and that it was okay to need help. That night, Marina called her sister and asked for the name of a therapist.

Now, sitting in the office, Marina is terrified that therapy will not work, that she will remain stuck in this place forever. But she is also, somewhere beneath the fear, hoping that someone can show her a way out of the loop she has been trapped in—that someone can help her find a way to remember Eduardo without falling apart.
